source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: The model plays both actor and world model. It proposes an action, predicts the next state, and a tree search (MCTS) uses self-scored rewards to pick paths. This is explicit mental simulation of options. It beats plain chain of thought on Blocksworld by a wide margin.
numbers: Blocksworld success, LLaMA-33B: CoT 0.17/0.02/0.00 on 2/4/6-step; RAP(10 iters) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42. GPT-4 CoT 0.50/0.63/0.40. Average RAP 64%. Intro cites GPT-3 at 1% vs humans 78% on Blocksworld.
quote: LLMs lack an internal world model to predict the world state and simulate long-term outcomes of actions
limits: Rewards were chosen by heuristics and exploratory runs. Search runs 10-20 iterations, so cost is many model calls. Blocksworld is a clean symbolic domain.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that simulate-then-choose beats single-shot generation for multi-step plans. Costly, so use it only when a cheap check fails (G1).

source: Hao et al. (2023) RAP, analysis section: full Blocksworld with Llama-2 70B
finding: With a stronger model the gain holds. CoT collapses on plans of six or more steps while RAP stays comparatively high. Authors conclude the framework helps regardless of base model strength.
numbers: Hard split, CoT row 0.22/0.14/0.02/0.02/0.00 by step count vs RAP(10) 0.67/0.76/0.74/0.48 (table partly garbled in text extraction).
limits: Table layout was damaged in text extraction, so only the pattern is reliable.
agent_relevance: Simulation helps most on long chains where first-guess generation fails, which matches RPD's claim that simulation is for checking a candidate path, not for easy cases.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Generate several candidate thoughts, have the model value each one (sure/maybe/impossible), and search with backtracking. A big jump on Game of 24 over chain of thought. The jump is mostly breadth plus self-evaluation, and it needs a strong model.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC(k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%, CoT best-of-100 49%. GPT-3.5 + ToT only 19%.
limits: Shallow trees (3 steps). Self-valuation is the model grading itself, which G5 warns about. Gain shrinks sharply with a weaker model.
agent_relevance: Shows a candidate-then-evaluate loop works, but best-of-100 CoT at 49% means part of the gain is just more samples. Compare against sample-matched baselines.

source: Liu et al. (2022) Mind's Eye: Grounded Language Model Reasoning Through Simulation
finding: A text-to-code step turns a physics question into a simulation in MuJoCo. The simulator output is injected into the prompt. This is mental simulation outsourced to a real engine. Accuracy rises a lot on a 39-task physics benchmark (UTOPIA).
numbers: Average absolute gain 27.9% zero-shot and 46.0% few-shot across 39 sub-tasks. Vanilla GPT-3 175B: 24% zero-shot, 38.2% few-shot. Few-shot scaling curve of vanilla models is nearly flat.
limits: Needs a domain simulator and a trained text-to-code front end (200,000 text-code pairs). Physics only.
agent_relevance: When a real simulator exists, calling it beats the model imagining outcomes. Our agent should prefer executed checks over imagined ones where possible (G2, G3).

source: Gu et al. (2025) Is Your LLM Secretly a World Model of the Internet? WebDreamer
finding: The agent proposes candidate actions, imagines the outcome of each in words with a world model, scores them, and then acts. It beats the reactive agent and nearly matches real tree search, at far lower cost and without irreversible actions.
numbers: Success rate % (VisualWebArena / Online-Mind2Web / Mind2Web-Live): reactive 17.6/26.0/20.2; tree search 26.2/-/-; WebDreamer GPT-4o 23.6/37.0/25.0; Qwen2-VL-7B 17.2/31.0/19.2; Qwen2-VL-72B 21.0/31.0/18.3; Dreamer-7B (trained) 21.9/35.0/24.0. Relative gain over reactive 34.1% (VWA), 42.3%, 23.8%. Shopping tasks: steps 4.5 vs 11.4 for tree search; seconds 179.4 vs 785.7.
limits: Small untrained world models (Qwen2-VL-7B) add almost nothing on VWA (17.2 vs 17.6). Tree search on real interactions still wins on VWA. A 100-task subset was used for some runs.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to RPD step 3 (imagine a candidate action before committing). Gains depend on world-model quality, so small models should not be trusted as simulators.

source: Chae et al. (2025, ICLR) Web Agents with World Models (WMA)
finding: First shows that LLMs predict next states poorly, then shows that giving the true next state makes action choice much better. A trained world model that writes only the state differences improves policy choice without retraining the policy.
numbers: Next-state prediction vs distractor: average 54.75% across LLMs. GPT-4o action selection: 53% with state only, 73% when next state is given. WebArena with GPT-4o-mini: WMA 16.6% vs CoT 13.1%. Gain over CoT with GPT-4o: +29.7% (WMA) vs +28.0% (tree search with oracle states). Cost per task: tree search $2.7 and 748.3 s; WMA $0.4 and 140.3 s.
limits: Shopping domain improved least; the authors blame the large state space. Absolute success stays low (16.6%).
agent_relevance: Quantifies the key point of mental simulation: a correct predicted outcome lifts option choice by about 20 points. A wrong prediction would cost the same. Prediction quality is the bottleneck.

source: Mei et al. (2026, ICLR) R-WoM: Retrieval-augmented World Model for Computer-use Agents
finding: LLMs predict the immediate next state well but drift over a full procedure. Grounding the imagined rollout in retrieved tutorials restores most of the lost accuracy and improves end-to-end success.
numbers: Next-state identification overall 77.0 (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B), 81.0 (Claude-3.5), 86.0 (Claude-3.7). Full-procedure plan alignment without retrieval 50.0/55.0/65.0, with retrieval 90.0/85.0/95.0. End-to-end OSWorld: Claude-3.7 vanilla 28.47, RAG 27.76, WebDreamer 31.24, R-WoM 38.54 (+23.4%); WebArena 28.92/32.75/31.86/34.58.
limits: Plan alignment is judged by an LLM (Claude-3.7-Sonnet). Needs good tutorials; a separate test covers tutorial-scarce cases. Three runs per cell, with noise of 1 to 3 points.
agent_relevance: Simulation is reliable for one step and unreliable for long horizons. Keep imagined rollouts short and anchor them to retrieved real cases, which is also how RPD works (experience supplies the expectancies).

source: Yu et al. (2026) ProAct: Agentic Lookahead in Interactive Environments
finding: States that LLM agents fail at long-horizon planning mainly because small errors compound when they simulate future states. Fix: train on reasoning chains distilled from real environment search trees, so the model learns foresight without runtime search. A 4B model rivals closed models on 2048 and Sokoban.
numbers: Table 1 examples: GPT-5 2048 scores 4040.0 (4x4), 1184.0 (3x3), 6962.0 (3072 variant); Sokoban base 1.89. Claude-4.5-Sonnet 2048 4x4 166.7; Sokoban base 1.06. Trained-4B numbers not extracted.
limits: Requires training, so it is outside our no-training constraint. I read the abstract, intro and part of the results only.
agent_relevance: Gives a competing explanation for why imagined lookahead fails (compounding error) and a hint that pre-training on grounded search can substitute for run-time simulation. For us: cap rollout depth and verify against real state.

source: Chang, Chandra, Hsu, Kuo (2026, AAMAS) MENSA: Mental Simulation for In-Context Policy Improvement in LLM Agents
finding: The LLM forecasts the next few action-state pairs, and the forecasts are used to retrieve similar past experiences into the prompt. This is recognition by simulation: imagine ahead, then match to stored cases. Large gains on ScienceWorld and NetHack over ReAct, Reflexion and SSO.
numbers: ScienceWorld adaptation, GPT-4o-mini: ReAct 22.4, Reflexion 25.9, SSO 54.5, MENSA 70.3 (+15.8). Phi-3-small +32.4 over SSO; Phi-3-mini +11.9. Transfer: +18.6 (Llama-3-8B), +19.9 (Gemma-2-9B). NetHack GPT-4o-mini: ReAct 12.0, SSO 10.0, MENSA 50.0 (+40.0). Wilcoxon test over 89 scores across 18 task classes.
quote: increasing the number of forecast steps beyond 3 negatively impacts both performance and token costs
limits: Best forecast depth was 3 steps. More steps hurt because later forecasts are wrong and extra text overwhelms the model. Retrieval ablation: target-based first 45.0 vs state-based only 41.4. Experience ordering mattered by 2 points. Single seed (42).
agent_relevance: Best direct analogue of RPD found: simulate a short way ahead (3 steps), retrieve matching experience, act. Shows a short horizon is optimal, as in expert simulations of only a few steps.

source: Lin et al. (2023, NeurIPS) SwiftSage: Fast and Slow Thinking for Complex Interactive Tasks
finding: A small fast module acts by pattern (like RPD simple match). A large model plans only when a rule detects trouble (an exception or no progress). It beats ReAct, Reflexion and SayCan on ScienceWorld at under half the tokens per action.
numbers: ScienceWorld overall (GPT-4): SwiftSage 84.68, Reflexion 45.34, ReAct 36.43, SayCan 33.82, DRRN 15.56. GPT-3.5: SwiftSage 62.22, SayCan 25.22, Reflexion 23.40, ReAct 19.76. Swift-only 49.22. Tokens per action 757 vs 1856 to 2983. 30 tasks, first 10 variations each (270 runs).
limits: Only ScienceWorld. Swift module is fine-tuned on oracle trajectories, so it is trained, not prompted. Switch rule is hand-written. Read via the arXiv HTML page.
agent_relevance: An existing agent loop built on the recognition-first, deliberate-on-trouble pattern. Matches our G1 (doubt only on a signal). The code-owned switch rule is the part to copy.

source: Goebel et al. (2026) Agentic LLM Planning via Step-Wise PDDL Simulation
finding: Letting an LLM execute one action at a time in a real simulator, observe the state, and reset gave only a small gain over writing the whole plan at once. The feedback was self-judged, with no external check on progress.
numbers: 102 IPC Blocksworld instances, 180 s budget: Fast Downward lama-first 85.3% (87 solved), seq-sat-lama-2011 85.3%, direct LLM (Claude Haiku 4.5) 63.7% (65), agentic LLM 66.7% (68). Agentic costs 5.7 times more tokens per solution. On one hard block agentic 20% vs direct 50%.
limits: One small model, one domain. Plans shorter than the baseline's suggest recall of training data.
agent_relevance: Walk-through simulation helps little when the agent must judge its own progress. Gains in coding come from compiler and test signals. Supports G2 and G3: only simulation with an external check counts.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models
finding: Frozen LLMs rarely produce executable plans even in simple Blocksworld, while untrained people do well. This is the baseline that the world-model and simulation papers try to beat.
numbers: Average autonomous plan success about 3%. Plan generation: human baseline 78% (39 of 50 participants valid), and 89.7% (35 of 39) of valid plans were optimal. 600 instances for most tests, 500 for plan generalization. GPT-3 and Instruct-GPT3 near 1 to 8% on Blocksworld plan generation.
limits: Older models (GPT-3, BLOOM). Numbers are far lower than current models. Human sample was small and preliminary.
agent_relevance: Humans solve this by quick recognition plus mental walk-through, the RPD pair. It sets a human anchor (78%) for any scaffold that claims to imitate it.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Position paper with data. GPT-4 alone makes executable plans rarely. The same model, used as an idea generator inside a loop with an external sound verifier, does much better. The model proposes, code verifies, and the critique is sent back.
numbers: GPT-4 about 12% executable plans on average. With VAL as verifier and back-prompting: Blocksworld 82% within 15 rounds, Logistics 70%, obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld about 10%.
quote: only about 12% of the plans that the best LLM (GPT-4) generates are actually executable
limits: Results cited from the authors' other papers. The loop works only where plausible candidates can be generated at all (Mystery BW stays near 10%).
agent_relevance: The best-evidenced shape for first workable option plus check: generator plus external simulator-verifier. This is the form of mental simulation we can trust.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: When GPT-4 critiques its own graph-colouring answers, accuracy collapses. With a sound external verifier it rises, but the content of the feedback hardly matters; extra attempts explain the gain.
numbers: Direct prompting baseline 16%. Self-critique back-prompting: 1 of 100 correct. Sound verifier: nearly 40%. Binary feedback, one error or all errors gave insignificant differences. Counting any correct answer in the chain also gave about 40%.
limits: One task (graph colouring), one model, 100 instances.
agent_relevance: Imagined self-evaluation of a candidate is unreliable. A real check is a stop rule more than a teacher. Fits G2 and G5, and warns that a simulated walk-through by the same model is weak evidence.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Code: Reasoning with a Language Model-Augmented Code Emulator
finding: The model writes a program. Lines that run are executed by a real interpreter. Lines that cannot run (fuzzy, semantic) are emulated by the model, which simulates the result. A hybrid of true execution and imagined execution.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard: Chain of Code 84%, a gain of 12 points over Chain of Thought, above average human raters.
limits: Gain is smaller when emulation carries most of the work. Reported as an average over BIG-Bench Hard tasks.
agent_relevance: A concrete pattern for mental simulation inside a loop: execute what can be executed, simulate only the rest, and mark which parts were imagined.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: MCTS over agent actions with model-based value estimates and self-reflection on failed branches. It sets a high pass rate on HumanEval and improves WebShop. Ablations show which part matters.
numbers: HumanEval GPT-4 pass@1 92.7%. HotPotQA exact match ablation (5 children, 50 trajectories): LATS full 0.63; without reflection 0.58; DFS instead of MCTS 0.42; without LM heuristic 0.37; ToT 0.39; RAP 0.54. Abstract: WebShop gain of 22.1 with GPT-3.5.
limits: Many model calls per task. The value heuristic is the model's own judgment. Read results and ablation tables, not every section.
agent_relevance: The model-based value heuristic is the largest single piece (0.63 to 0.37 when removed). Reflection adds a small amount (5 points).

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: After a failed trial the agent writes a verbal lesson into memory and retries. This is post-hoc review of a failed course of action, a cousin of RPD's expectancy violation and re-diagnosis.
numbers: ALFWorld: ReAct + Reflexion completes 130 of 134 tasks. HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80% for GPT-4 baseline.
limits: Needs a clear success or failure signal between trials. Later work (c14, c10) shows gains depend on external signals.
agent_relevance: Revision after a real failing outcome is supported. It matches G2 and works as the re-diagnosis step when a simulated path breaks.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: The model first writes relevant past problems from its own memory, then solves the new one. That is a prompt-only version of recognition (match to a prior case). It beats zero-shot and hand-written few-shot chain of thought on several tasks.
numbers: Abstract-level only: outperforms 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench. Per-task figures not extracted.
limits: I read the abstract and intro only. Self-generated exemplars can be wrong, and the gain depends on model size.
agent_relevance: Cheapest way to give RPD's recognise-a-typical-case step to a frozen model. Covered in more depth by the analogical access subfield; only noted here.

source: Danial, Smith, Veitch, Khan (2019) On the realization of the recognition-primed decision model for artificial agents
finding: A full computational RPD agent. Recognition uses a Markov logic network trained on past cases. Diagnosis uses ontology feature matching when the case is new. Mental simulation is a Bayesian network that scores whether a course of action will work. Checked against human offshore fire-evacuation data.
numbers: Human data from Smith's virtual-environment study, 36 participants (17 trained over several sessions, 19 with one session). Agent fitted on 80% of 17 trained participants' data, tested on 20%. Agreement reported by example cases, not by one accuracy score.
limits: No single accuracy or effect size. One narrow domain. The simulation step was reduced to a plan that watches for violated expectancies. Authors say further work is needed.
agent_relevance: An older, non-LLM blueprint for all three RPD stages. The weak part was the simulation module, which supports treating simulation as an add-on check.

source: Goecks and Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformers for Accelerated Course of Action Development
finding: A military course-of-action tool: the LLM writes one COA from doctrine plus mission text, the commander reviews it, and feedback refines it. The review step is the human version of RPD's evaluate-by-simulation. The model beat reinforcement-learning baselines.
numbers: StarCraft II TigerClaw scenario, 50 rollouts per condition; expert human 15 trials. Best COA-GPT variant (vision, after two feedback rounds) scored 3.4% lower than the human expert on mean reward, with less variance. The LLM COAs had more friendly casualties than the human.
limits: Game environment, not a real battlefield. The human expert controlled units in real time while the model gave a single plan, so the comparison is uneven.
agent_relevance: An LLM gives a first workable course of action and is improved by short criticism cycles, as in commander studies. Casualty cost shows workable is not the same as good.

source: From Word to World: Can Large Language Models be Implicit Text-based World Models? (2025)
finding: Tests how well LLMs predict the next state in text environments and whether imagined rollouts match real ones. Fine-tuned small models are accurate in rule-bound worlds and weak in open-ended ones. Checking a candidate action before running it helps a little.
numbers: Next-state exact match (ALFWorld/SciWorld/TextWorld/WebShop): Claude-sonnet-4.5 zero-shot 64.73/56.83/17.70/58.80; 3-shot 77.04/73.08/49.12/56.65; Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned 99.87/98.60/70.60/79.05. Consistency ratio of world-model rollouts to real (Qwen2.5-7B): ALFWorld 0.96, SciWorld 0.91, TextWorld 0.92, WebShop 0.67. Pre-execution checks on WebShop, GPT-4-turbo 17.73 to 33.33 with 2 checks (+15.60); GPT-4o 29.36 to 32.41 with 2 checks, 36.70 with 50.
limits: Not monotonic in number of checks. Verification changes the agent's context, which shifts its actions. Read first 100,000 of 135,000 characters. Text environments only; world models get the full initial state in two of the environments. Author list not captured.
agent_relevance: Pre-execution simulation works but with a small budget (2 to 10 checks). Rollouts drift in open-ended worlds, so trust them only where rules are crisp.

source: Vafa et al. (2024) Evaluating the World Model Implicit in a Generative Model
finding: Models that score well on usual next-token and path tests for navigation, Othello and logic puzzles have world models that are far less coherent than they look. This makes them fragile when the task differs slightly.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures extracted.
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session.
agent_relevance: A warning that a good first-step prediction does not prove a usable simulator. Test the simulation on perturbed cases before relying on it (G3).

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLM-Modulo, Mystery Blocksworld finding
finding: On an obfuscated version of Blocksworld the generator-verifier loop barely helps. If the model cannot produce plausible candidates, a verifier cannot rescue it. Recognition (a good first candidate) is the limiting factor.
numbers: Mystery Blocksworld about 10% after back-prompting, vs 82% on standard Blocksworld; Logistics 70%.
limits: Taken from the position paper's summary of earlier results.
agent_relevance: In RPD terms, simulation can only prune candidates that recognition already supplies. Where the problem is unfamiliar, a diagnose or reframe step must come before simulation.

source: Chae et al. (2025) WMA, per-domain efficiency read-out
finding: The world model is used only to rank a few sampled candidate actions. This is cheaper than search and does not need backtracking in the live environment. Domain differences are large.
numbers: Shopping 20.8% vs tree search 28.1%; CMS 14.3 vs 16.5; Reddit 10.5 vs 10.5; Gitlab 13.3 vs 13.3; Map 26.8 vs 25.8 (GPT-4o policy). Cost $0.4 vs $2.7; time 140.3 s vs 748.3 s.
limits: Tree search numbers come from a different paper's runs (Koh et al.), so the match is not fully controlled.
agent_relevance: Simulating a handful of candidates matches full search in 3 of 5 domains. That supports a few-options, simulate-each-briefly loop and not an exhaustive one.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, GPT-3.5 versus GPT-4
finding: Scale matters: the same method that gets 74% with GPT-4 gets 19% with GPT-3.5 on Game of 24. Self-evaluation quality is the limit. Also IO + Refine (k=10) reaches 27%, below ToT.
numbers: Game of 24: ToT GPT-4 b=5 74%; GPT-3.5 19%; IO+Refine k=10 27%; IO best of 100 33%.
limits: Authors changed the prompt to 3-shot to make GPT-3.5 work at all.
agent_relevance: Imagined evaluation is a capability that appears only in stronger models, so test it per model before relying on it.

source: Literature search for LLM tests of RPD itself (WebSearch, 2026-10-26)
finding: Searched for studies that test language models on Klein's RPD paradigm directly (fireground cases, first-option satisficing, commanders against LLMs). Found none. Related work is limited to symbolic RPD agents (Danial 2019, c19), LLM COA tools (c20) and general world-model planning (c05, c06, c09).
numbers: No study found with fireground or incident-command scenarios scored against human experts.
limits: Search engine returns US results only and finds mostly abstracts. Absence of results here is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: The LLM case for RPD rests on indirect evidence. Any claim that our scaffold matches expert intuition needs our own test.

source: Stechly et al. (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong, sampling comparison
finding: The paper compares iterative back-prompting against plain re-sampling. The gain comes from having many chances, not from the critique. This is a competing explanation for improvements credited to simulate-and-revise loops.
numbers: Fifteen iterations vs one attempt: success near 40% with a sound verifier stopping the chain, and the same near 40% for any-correct-in-chain regardless of feedback type.
limits: Graph colouring only.
agent_relevance: Control for number of attempts when claiming a simulation step helps: always compare against best-of-N with the same calls.

source: Gu et al. (2025) WebDreamer, world-model size and training
finding: Training a 7B world model on synthesized data (Dreamer-7B) adds a few points over the untrained 7B and rivals GPT-4o on two online benchmarks. The untrained 72B is no better than the 7B on Mind2Web-Live.
numbers: Fine-tuning Qwen2-VL-7B to Dreamer-7B: +4.7 (VWA), +4.0 (Online-Mind2Web), +4.8 (Mind2Web-Live). Qwen2-VL-72B on Mind2Web-Live 18.3 vs 7B 19.2.
limits: Online benchmark runs are noisy (about 100 tasks).
agent_relevance: Model size is not what makes a good simulator; domain-specific training or grounding is. Without training we should lean on retrieval and executed checks.
